html:
The Code of Hammurabi is a set of Babylonian laws issued by King Hammurabi around 1754 BCE and carved on a black stone stele more than two metres tall. It is the best known law code of the ancient Near East. The date follows the Middle Chronology.

At the top of the stele, Hammurabi stands before the sun god Shamash, god of justice. Below, in Akkadian cuneiform, come a prologue, about 282 laws, and an epilogue in which the king says he wrote them so that the strong would not oppress the weak.

The laws cover daily life in the Old Babylonian kingdom:

  • Trade, loans, wages and prices.
  • Marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption.
  • Builders whose houses collapse, doctors whose patients die, and farmers who neglect their dykes.

Punishments depend on rank. Harm to a free man of equal rank was often paid back in kind, "an eye for an eye". Harm to a commoner or a slave was usually paid with silver. It is not clear how far judges actually followed the code; it may have been as much a statement of royal justice as a working law book.

About six hundred years later, an Elamite king raided Babylonia and carried the stele off to Susa in Elam as a trophy. French archaeologists found it there in 1901, and it is now in the Louvre in Paris. It draws on older traditions such as the Code of Ur-Nammu.
